title: Leadership
blurb: Influence, decisions, feedback and teams: principles for leading work you don't fully control.

cards.prompt: What is psychological safety, and what is it not?
cards.answer: A shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking: asking questions, admitting mistakes, raising concerns. It is not niceness, comfort or lowered standards. Edmondson pairs it with accountability: high safety plus high standards is the learning zone, and high safety with low standards is just comfort.
points: Shared belief that interpersonal risk is safe
Not niceness or lowered standards
Safety plus accountability = learning zone
Safety without standards = comfort zone

cards.prompt: Heifetz distinguishes technical problems from adaptive challenges. What's the difference, and what's the classic leadership failure?
cards.answer: A technical problem has a known solution that an expert or authority can implement. An adaptive challenge requires the people who have the problem to learn and change their values, habits or loyalties, so no one can solve it for them. The classic failure is treating an adaptive challenge as a technical one, such as buying a tool to fix a culture problem.
points: Technical: known solution, expert can apply it
Adaptive: the people with the problem must change
Authority can't solve adaptive challenges by itself
Failure: applying technical fixes to adaptive problems
cards.source: Ronald Heifetz, Leadership Without Easy Answers (1994)

cards.prompt: Cohen and Bradford's model of influence without authority: how does it work?
cards.answer: Treat the other person as a potential ally. Clarify what you need, then understand their world: their pressures, goals and what they value, their 'currencies'. Influence comes from exchange: offer what they value (help, information, recognition, access) in return for what you need, and build the relationship so the exchanges continue.
points: Assume a potential ally
Clarify your goals
Diagnose their world and currencies
Exchange what they value for what you need
Invest in the relationship

cards.prompt: Situational leadership: the four styles, and what decides which to use.
cards.answer: Directing, coaching, supporting, delegating. The choice depends on the person's development level on that specific task: their competence and commitment, not their seniority.
cards.why: The same person can need directing on a new task and delegating on a familiar one.

cards.answer: Situation, Behavior, Impact. Name when and where, describe the observable behavior (not character or intent), and say what effect it had. Then ask for their view.
Recommend, Agree, Perform, Input, Decide. Exactly one person holds the D.
cards.why: Most decision gridlock comes from unclear D, or from too many people who believe they hold an A (a veto).
cards.source: Rogers & Blenko, Who Has the D? (HBR, 2006)

cards.answer: Forming, storming, norming, performing, plus adjourning, added in 1977.
cards.why: Storming is normal, not a sign the team is failing. A team skips it only by suppressing conflict.

cards.prompt: What is Chesterton's fence, and how does it apply to legacy rules and systems?
cards.answer: Don't remove a fence until you know why it was put up. With an odd validation rule, a manual step or a strange table, find out what problem it solved. Then decide: the reason may be gone, or the fence may be holding up something you can't see.
points: Understand why before removing
Legacy oddities often encode past failures
The reason may have expired, or may still hold
Then decide deliberately

cards.prompt: 'Disagree and commit': what does it require of you before and after the decision?
cards.answer: Before: state your disagreement fully and clearly while the decision is still open. After: commit to making the decision succeed. No relitigating, no quiet foot-dragging, no 'I told you so'. Reopen it only with new information, through the channel that made it.
points: Voice disagreement fully before the decision
Then commit to making it work
No relitigating or passive resistance
Reopen only with new information
cards.source: Intel management practice (Andy Grove); Bezos, 2016 shareholder letter

cards.prompt: Your sponsor wants a visible win in 90 days, but the foundational work will take a year. How do you handle it?
cards.answer: Don't choose between them. Pick a thin end-to-end slice on a high-visibility use case that also delivers one reusable piece of the foundation. Make foundation progress visible with a few honest metrics. Set expectations explicitly with a roadmap that shows what the win does and doesn't prove. Avoid one-off hacks that create debt, and raise risks early rather than at the deadline.
points: A thin end-to-end slice that also builds foundation
Choose a high-visibility use case
Make foundation progress visible
Explicit roadmap and expectations
Avoid one-off hacks; surface risks early

cards.prompt: A vendor says a capability you need is 'supported.' How do you hold them to it before and after you sign?
cards.answer: Turn the capability into testable acceptance criteria in your own terms: the systems, versions and scope it must work on. Require a proof of concept on your own environment and data, with a known test case and its expected result. Ask for reference customers with a similar setup, and separate what ships today from what's on the roadmap. Put the criteria, the timeline and the remedy for failure into the contract.
points: Testable acceptance criteria in your own terms (systems, versions, scope)
Proof of concept on your own environment and data, with an expected result
Reference customers with a similar setup
Separate what ships today from the roadmap
Criteria, timeline and remedy in the contract
cards.source: Standard procurement practice (acceptance testing, proof of concept)
